Ananthanarayanan 2019 (Uber, self-reported): against the same oracle, Speculate-all reaches up to 15x the 50th-percentile turnaround (up to 24x at P99), and Single-Queue, one change at a time, reaches 80x at P50 at 500 changes per hour.

Ananthanarayanan 2019 (Uber, self-reported): with two concurrent, potentially conflicting changes there is a 5% chance of a real conflict, rising to 40% with sixteen, and changes one to ten hours stale have a 10% to 20% chance of making the mainline red.

Ananthanarayanan 2019 (Uber, self-reported): SubmitQueue's throughput slowdown against the oracle is up to 60%, falling to around 20% with 500 workers; Single-Queue's slowdown is 95%.
Ananthanarayanan 2019 (Uber, self-reported): the conflict analyzer improves the oracle's turnaround by up to 60%, but only 20% for the Optimistic approach because the iOS build graph is very deep.

Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019: batch testing saves 72% of test executions against testing each commit alone, in a simulation of three Ericsson projects (14k commits over nine months) at a 2.8% culprit rate with batches up to 9.
note: The abstract gives 42% for the flakiness saving; the body gives 41% for the best project (line 56), which x32-0307 uses.

claim: Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019: with a flake rate 1.37 times higher, a batch of 4 saves 14% of executions against 41% without flakiness, and Project C's best batch falls from 9 (72% saved) to 4 (41% saved) once flaky failures are counted.

Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019: the higher the culprit rate the smaller the most cost-effective batch; Project A, with a culprit rate 2.4 times Project C's, saves 46% at batch size 4, while Project C saves 72% at batch size up to 9.
Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019: savings are logarithmic in batch size, with batch 2 saving 34%, 34% and 44% of executions for Projects A, B and C, and most of the saving falling up to batch 4.
Najafi, Rigby and Shang 2019 state the condition for batching at Ericsson: each commit under test should be independent of the other commits.

Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023: BatchAll keeps the actual average feedback time with up to 91% fewer machines than TestAll on Chrome (9,524 changes in January 2021, build failure rate about 8.5%; 5 to 375 machines in scale).

Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023: Batch4 saves 71.89% of machines on Chrome (Batch2 47.93%), but on Ericsson Batch4 needs 8 machines for the same average feedback time, a -14.29% reduction against the baseline.
Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023: BatchAll reduces machines by 28.57% at Ericsson (5 machines) and by 90.78% at Chrome (20 machines) for the same average feedback time.

Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023: at Ericsson TestAll needs 7 machines for an average feedback time of 8.33 hours, and going from 6 to 7 machines speeds it up 2.65 times but from 7 to 8 only 1.5 times; at Chrome TestAll needs 217 machines for 36.48 minutes.
Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023: constant batches plateau with a relatively high feedback time, and TestAll outperforms them when machines far exceed the baseline.
Fallahzadeh, Bavand and Rigby 2023 state two conditions: the Chrome build failure rate of 8.5% is 'well below the 40% threshold', and 'all changes can be batched and none lead to merge conflict'.

Fallahzadeh, Rigby and Adams 2025: test selection cuts machine usage by up to 66%, and batching by up to 88%.

note: Counts build test executions, not waiting time. This is the 2020 Concordia thesis, the master's version of the IEEE TSE 2021 work; the TSE paper itself was not opened.

Rust forge rollup procedure (fetched 2026-11-19): when a rollup fails, the failure is bisected to one PR from the log, that PR is unapproved, and the rollup is closed and recreated without it.
